Learning Objectives
Assess the structure and function of DNA as the basis of heredity.
Apply the genetic basis of diseases and genetic therapies.
Determine the role and potential of modern molecular technology in aiding diagnosis,
prognosis, and therapy.
Describe the scope and clinical relevance of molecular orthopaedics.
DNA Structure
Genetics is the study of heredity. This lesson explores genetics at the molecular level.1 The
study of genetics in the context of orthopaedics has been termed molecular orthopaedics.2
In all organisms, apart from certain viruses, genetic information is stored as DNA3 (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration shows the DNA double helix condensing around histones to form
nucleosomes, which then are packaged into individual chromosomes within the nucleus of the
cell. (Reproduced with permission from Minchin S, Lodge J: Understanding biochemistry:
Structure and function of nucleic acids. Essays Biochem 2019;63[4]:433-456.)
In eukaryotic organisms, DNA is organized into chromosomes that reside within the nucleus of
the cell. Each chromosome consists of a single molecule of DNA and its associated proteins. A
small amount of extranuclear DNA resides in mitochondria.
Each human, nucleated, diploid cell normally has two sets of 23 homologous chromosomes,
one set inherited from each parent. (Spermatozoa and ova have only one copy of each
chromosome and are said to be haploid). In males and females, 22 pairs of chromosomes,
known as autosomes, are the same and are numbered 1 to 22 in decreasing order of size. The
remaining pair of chromosomes are the sex chromosomes, XX in females and XY in males. The
normal chromosomal complement is called a karyotype.
DNA is a polymer, in which sugar (deoxyribose) molecules are covalently linked by
phosphodiester bonds to form a sugar-phosphate backbone. Purine (adenine [A], guanine [G])
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Genetics, Gene Expression, and Epigenetics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002109
2/18

and pyrimidine (cytosine [C], thymine [T]) bases are covalently linked to and project from the
sugar-phosphate backbone. The polymer formed often is referred to as a strand of DNA.
DNA strands have polarity. One end is the so-called 5’ (five prime) end, and the other end is the
3’ end. This nomenclature is derived from the numbering of the carbon atoms on the
deoxyribose component of DNA.
DNA normally exists in a form in which two strands of DNA align side by side in opposite
polarity to each other and twist to form a helix—the famous double helix of DNA. The
association between the two strands of the helix is stabilized by hydrogen bonding between
the purines and pyrimidines that project from the sugar-phosphate backbone of each strand
of DNA. Hydrogen bonding involves one purine bonding across the helix with one pyrimidine
on the opposite strand of DNA; adenine binds to thymine (A-T) and guanine binds to cytosine
(G-C). The sequence of purine and pyrimidine bases in one strand of the DNA determines the
sequence in the other strand; the two strands are said to be complementary to each other.
These purine-pyrimidine associations are known as base pairs and often are used as units of
DNA size. For example, the entire human genetic complement (human genome) comprises
approximately 3 × 109 base pairs of DNA. Mitochondria have only 16,500 base pairs of DNA.
Although hydrogen bonds are individually weak, so many of them exist in these long polymers,
that collectively, they ensure the stability of the double stranded DNA helix under normal
physiologic conditions. However, they are weak enough to become unzipped for the purposes
of DNA replication and transcription. The sequence of bases in DNA is critically important to its
genetic function.
Note that the bases adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine occasionally are referred to as
nucleotides. This vocabulary reflects the name for a purine or pyrimidine base covalently
linked to deoxyribose phosphate, which occurs within the larger structure of DNA.
DNA Replication
To serve as the genetic material of heredity, DNA must be replicated accurately and passed
from parent to daughter cells at each cell division. The complementary, double-strand nature
of DNA and the precision of base pairing allow it to perform this function.
DNA replication involves the separation of the two strands of DNA, each of which serves as a
template for the synthesis of a new, complementary strand of DNA by the enzyme DNA
polymerase. Each of the two new DNA molecules formed contain one strand of the pre-
existing DNA and one newly synthesized, complementary strand. This process is called
semiconservative replication.

During replication, DNA polymerase inserts bases into the growing strand of DNA that is being
synthesized in accordance with the base-pairing rules of A-T, G-C. This process ensures the
perpetuation of the correct base sequence; however, an incorrect base is inserted at a
frequency of approximately 1 in 105. This produces a point mutation, which may result in
disease even though cells possess DNA repair enzymes that can correct certain mutations. The
mutation rate is increased by exposure to various chemicals and types of radiation that cause
cancer.
Chromosomes are capped at each end by regions of DNA known as telomeres. Each time DNA
replicates, the telomeres become shorter. Telomere shortening is thought to underlie the
aging process and a number of age-related diseases.
DNA Function
One of the primary functions of DNA is to enable the synthesis of specific proteins. Discrete
stretches of DNA contain genetic information necessary for the synthesis of particular
proteins; these areas are coding regions known as genes. Other regions of the DNA control the
activities of the genes.
Only 1.2% of human DNA encodes proteins. The function of much of the rest is unknown;
however, at least some of these regions are important in regulating gene expression. The
noncoding regions of DNA of unknown function occasionally are referred to as junk DNA, a
term that is a subject of debate.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds and arranged in a
specific sequence. In mammalian cells, 20 different amino acids can be incorporated into a
newly synthesized protein chain. Each amino acid has a corresponding three-base sequence,
known as a codon, in DNA. For example, the codon GCT encodes the amino acid alanine, and
the codon CAG encodes the amino acid arginine. The four bases (guanine, cytosine, adenine,
and thymine) organized in codons of three bases allow for 43 or 64 permutations. What each
of these 64 codons signifies is known as the genetic code (Table 1).

With only 20 amino acids in proteins, the 64 codons allow for considerable redundancy.
Several amino acids, such as arginine and glycine, are represented by more than one codon.
Three stop codons terminate protein synthesis. Not all codons encoding a specific amino acid
are equally efficient in all types of cells.
The strand of DNA containing the codons that will be used to determine the amino acid
sequence in the final protein product is called the sense strand. The complementary strand is
called the antisense strand.
In mammalian cells, the sequence of bases within a gene that determines the amino acid
sequence of its cognate protein is not continuous, with rare exceptions. Instead, the coding
sequences (exons) are interrupted by intervening, noncoding sequences (introns). The latter
are removed during the process that leads to protein synthesis.

The genes of bacteria are continuous and have no introns. Mitochondrial DNA also has no
introns. This fact is consistent with the hypothesis that mitochondria are derived from
symbiotic bacteria that became incorporated into eukaryotic cells. Most genes encoding
histones also lack introns, an occurrence that is extremely rare in mammalian cells.
The synthesis of a specific protein occurs when the gene encoding that protein is switched on
and gene expression begins. The human genome is thought to contain 20,000 to 25,000 genes
that encode proteins. Usually, two copies of each gene are present, one on each homologous
chromosome.
The two copies of each gene may have differences in base sequence from each other.
Different versions of the same gene at the same chromosomal location are known as alleles.
Nearly all somatic cells in the body contain the same DNA. One exception is lymphocytes, in
which DNA is rearranged as part of the adaptive immune response. Different types of cells
express unique subsets of their 20,000 to 25,000 genes, which helps explain their different
phenotypes and functions. For example, chondrocytes express the gene Col2A1 (encoding type
II collagen, located on chromosome 12), which distinguishes them from almost all other cells.
Some genes, known as housekeeping genes, are expressed constitutively. For example,
glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase is a housekeeping enzyme encoded by a gene on the X
chromosome.
Gene expression begins when the sequence of bases in the DNA of a gene is copied during the
process of transcription into a molecule of pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA). Unlike DNA, RNA
contains ribose instead of deoxyribose in the sugar-phosphate backbone, and the pyrimidine
base uracil (U) instead of thymine (T). Some versions of the genetic code show codons
containing U in place of T. RNA does not form the large, stable helices of DNA, but it undergoes
localized base-pairing to generate various important, shorter secondary and tertiary
structures.
Transcription is driven by a sequence of DNA known as a promoter adjacent to the 5’ end of
the gene. This binds proteins called transcription factors that engage the enzyme RNA
polymerase II. Transcription factors of orthopaedic importance are RUNX2, which is essential
for the differentiation of osteoblasts and for skeletal morphogenesis, and SOX9, which is
essential for cartilage differentiation.
RNA polymerase II uses one strand of the DNA, the antisense strand, as a template for the
synthesis of pre-mRNA. The resulting base sequence of pre-mRNA is complementary to the
antisense strand of the DNA and, therefore, identical to that of the sense strand of the DNA
(except for the presence of U instead of T).

Pre-mRNA is then processed into mature RNA, a process that comprises several steps,
including biochemical modification of the 5’ end of the mRNA (known as capping), the removal
of intron sequences (splicing), and the addition of a long chain of 100 to 250 adenine bases to
the 3’ end of mRNA (polyadenylation) to produce a poly A tail.
Mature mRNA molecules then leave the nucleus and enter the cytoplasm (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Diagram shows the structure and expression of a protein-coding eukaryotic gene. The
DNA includes an untranslated region at the 5’ and 3’ ends and the introns and exons. The DNA
is transcribed into pre-messenger RNA and is processed by addition of the 5’ cap, splicing out
the introns and addition of the poly A tail. This mature messenger RNA is exported from the
nucleus into the cytoplasm. (Reproduced with permission from Minchin S, Lodge J:
Understanding biochemistry: Structure and function of nucleic acids. Essays Biochem
2019;63[4]:433-456.)
The genetic information in a mature mRNA molecule is used to assemble the precise sequence
of amino acids joined by peptide bonds that constitute the protein product. This process is
called translation. It makes use of two additional species of RNA: transfer RNA, which delivers
each specific amino acid to the growing peptide chain, and ribosomal RNA, which forms an
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Genetics, Gene Expression, and Epigenetics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002109
7/18

integral part of each ribosome, the organelle, where peptide bonds are formed as the protein
chain elongates.
In mammalian cells, translation starts at the site of the start codon AUG, with very rare
exceptions. Because this codon also signifies the amino acid methionine, the first amino acid
in newly synthesized proteins is methionine. In mitochondrial proteins, similar to those of
bacteria, N-formyl methionine is the first amino acid.
Translation stops when the ribosome encounters a stop codon (UAG, UAA or UGA) in the
mRNA, and the protein is released from the ribosome.
The transfer of genetic information from DNA to RNA and RNA to protein has been termed the
Central Dogma of Molecular Biology. Certain viruses, known as retroviruses, have RNA
genomes and possess a reverse transcriptase enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
Of all human genes, 95% are able to increase the number of different proteins they produce
via a process of alternative splicing. As described previously, the splicing of pre-mRNA removes
introns and joins together exons. Alternative splicing allows the joining of alternative exons
within the pre-mRNA, thereby producing mature mRNA encoding different, albeit related,
proteins. An estimated 20,000 to 25,000 genes of the human genome are able to generate
more than 100,000 different proteins via alternative splicing.
Gene expression is driven by adjacent promoter regions of DNA at the 5’ end of the gene.
Expression may be elevated further by additional stretches of DNA known as enhancers,
which, dissimilar from promoters, may lie a considerable distance away from the gene and
may reside 3’ or 5’ to the gene. Silencer regions of DNA inhibit gene expression by
sequestering transcription factors.
The human genome also contains approximately 14,000 pseudogenes, which are thought to
be former genes that have lost their ability to code for proteins.
The level of gene expression also can be regulated at the level of mRNA, and cells use various
types of noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to achieve this purpose. These types of ncRNA are generated
via the transcription of genes, but they are not translated into a protein product and,
therefore, are noncoding. Instead, they bind in a sequence-specific fashion to mRNA via base-
pairing and thereby inhibit translation or cause degradation of mRNA. This area of research is
very active and includes the discovery of many new types of ncRNA, including microRNA, small
inhibitory RNA, long ncRNA, and circular RNA.
Approximately 22,000 human genes encode RNA only and do not produce a protein product.
In addition to regulation at the level of transcription and translation, the physiologic levels and
functions of individual proteins may be regulated by posttranslational processing, secretion,
and breakdown (proteolysis). The repertoire of possible posttranslational modifications is very

large and includes acylation, hydroxylation, phosphorylation, and the covalent addition of
sugar (glycosylation).
Epigenetics
In addition to the DNA-based and RNA-based mechanisms already described, gene expression
can be regulated by epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms do not change the DNA
sequence but biochemically modify DNA and its associated proteins. Regardless, the changes
are heritable and passed on during cell division. The best-understood epigenetic changes are
DNA methylation and histone modification.4 Epigenetic changes are important in
development, homeostasis, disease, and behavior.
The methylation of DNA predominantly occurs at certain cytosine (C) residues and forms 5-
methylcytosine. Methylcytosine still can form a base pair with guanine; however, if
methylcytosine is present in the promoter or enhancer region of a gene, expression often is
repressed because key transcription factors are no longer able to bind there. Conversely, if
methylcytosine is present in the coding region of a gene, expression often is enhanced.
The DNA of each human cell is 2 meters long. This creates a packaging problem, which is
solved by condensing the DNA around certain proteins, including histones, to form chromatin.
In chromatin, DNA wraps around two copies of histones 2A, 2B, 3, and 4 to form nucleosomes.
Under the electron microscope, these nucleosomes create a characteristic beads-on-a-string
image.
If nucleosomes are packed densely, they form heterochromatin, within which DNA is not
available for transcription. The less condensed form is called euchromatin and is more
accessible to the machinery of gene expression.
The biochemical modification of histones provides another epigenetic mechanism for
controlling gene expression. Prominent histone modifications include methylation, acetylation,
phosphorylation, and ubiquitination. Depending on the circumstances, modifications of this
type may enhance or inhibit gene expression.
Compounds that alter the activities of histone-modifying enzymes hold therapeutic potential.
Several epigenetic drugs of this type have been approved by the FDA for the management of
certain cancers.
Genomics
The entirety of the DNA of an organism is known as its genome.

The Human Genome Project involved determining the precise sequence of the entire 3 billion
bases of the human genome. This project was declared complete in 2003; however, details
continue to be learned.
The analysis and interpretation of this information have given rise to the discipline of
genomics, which seeks to understand the role of genetics and gene interactions in health,
disease, and drug responses, as well as how organisms interact with their environments.
In medicine, genomics aids in the development of improved diagnostics, improves
understanding of disease, informs the development of more effective therapeutic strategies,
and provides better decision-making tools for patients and physicians. It also is valuable in the
context of precision medicine, in which therapies can be individualized and tailored based on a
patient’s genome.
Data from genome sequencing have facilitated the emergence of the genome-wide association
study, an approach that involves rapidly scanning markers across the complete genomes of
many individuals to find genetic variations associated with a particular disease. This
information can be used to develop better strategies to detect, manage, and prevent disease,
especially complex diseases involving many genes and environmental influences.
The success of genomics has spawned a large body of related disciplines, including proteomics
(the study of all the proteins in the body), transcriptomics (the study of all RNA), and
metabolomics (the study of all metabolites).
These activities generate vast amounts of big data, the analysis of which engages information
science and computer science and, increasingly, artificial intelligence.
The word orthogenomics has been coined to refer to those components of the genome of
relevance to orthopaedic science.5
Genetic Basis of Disease
Genetic disorders6-8 can be caused by a mutation in one gene (monogenic disorder),
mutations in multiple genes (multifactorial inheritance disorder), a combination of gene
mutations and environmental factors (complex diseases), or damage to chromosomes
(changes in the number or structure of entire chromosomes).
Genetic diseases caused by single gene defects occasionally are referred to as Mendelian
diseases.
Genetic disorders typically are rare and often are difficult to manage. A complete list of genetic
diseases can be found at the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man website.9 This website

9/3/26, 4:18 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002109
10/18

contains a continuously updated catalog of human genes, genetic disorders, and traits. More
than 6,000 Mendelian disorders are known.
A mutation is a change in the sequence of purine and pyrimidine bases within a gene or its
regulatory elements. Several types of mutations have been identified.
Point mutation—A change, insertion, or deletion in a single base of DNA. A point mutation
can be silent, in which the target protein is unchanged; a nonsense, in which the target
protein is interrupted by a newly introduced stop codon; or a missense, which results in a
change in the amino acid composition of a protein. Orthopaedic examples of diseases
caused by point mutations include fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva and achondroplasia.
Frameshift mutation—The result of the addition or deletion of genetic material that causes a
misreading of all subsequent codons in the gene. Because DNA is read in the unit of the
codon that is composed of three base pairs, an insertion or deletion in a number that is not a
multiple of three will result in frameshift.
Translocation—Movement of genetic material from one chromosome to a different
chromosome. Translocations can alter DNA transcription and result in the formation of
abnormal proteins that cause cancers, such as Ewing sarcoma.
Inheritance patterns of genetic disease
Autosomal mutation—A gene mutation located on a chromosome other than the X or Y
chromosome
Sex-linked mutation—A gene mutation located on the X or Y chromosome; a disease caused
by an X-linked mutation usually is restricted to males because they have only one X
chromosome.
Dominant mutation—The mutation of a single allele of a gene that is sufficient to cause an
abnormal phenotype of the organism carrying that allele. Such mutations are referred to as
dominant negative.
Recessive mutation—A mutation that must occur in both alleles of a gene to cause an
abnormal phenotype of the organism carrying the two alleles.

Polymorphisms—DNA contains considerable variation outside of the well-defined mutations
that cause specific diseases. These variations, known as polymorphisms, are not pathogenic
but may influence the susceptibility to or protection from specific diseases. Polymorphisms are
more common than mutations. A variant needs to be present in the population at a frequency
of at least 1% to be considered a polymorphism.
Much interest has been focused on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs or snips) that
involve a single base change. SNPs are being investigated in various orthopaedic contexts,
such as susceptibility to osteoporosis, fracture, tendon injury, intervertebral disk degeneration,
aseptic loosening, and osteoarthritis.10 An estimated 4 to 5 million SNPs are present in the
human genome.
SNPs also may help predict responses to therapy and, therefore, may aid in the development
of precision medicine as applied to orthopaedic patients.
A haplotype refers to a set of genetic variations that occur in close proximity along a stretch of
DNA. The International HapMap Project is producing a haplotype map of the human genome.
Genetic Therapy
Gene therapy is an emerging technology in the management of genetic diseases. It involves
the use of a vector to transfer a normal (often called wild-type) gene, usually its
complementary DNA (cDNA) into a patient to compensate for a mutated gene. The vector
often is a modified, harmless virus.
If the mutation is recessive and the transferred gene (transgene) is expressed appropriately in
the correct cells, a therapeutic effect is expected.
With a dominant negative mutation, the mutant gene needs to be suppressed before a wild-
type gene can be effective. Various strategies exist for this process, including the use of ncRNA.

9/3/26, 4:18 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002109
13/18

Gene delivery can be used to manage acquired and genetic diseases. Clinical trials are
underway for gene therapy in patients with osteoarthritis.
Gene editing provides an alternative approach in the management of genetic diseases.11
Rather than introduce additional genetic material into the body, gene editing corrects
mutations within the defective gene. The advantage is that the corrected gene is fully native;
its introns are intact, and the regulatory elements are those of the normal gene.
The most advanced technology for gene editing is provided by clustered regularly interspaced
short palindromic repeats (CRISPRs) and CRISPR-associated protein, a nuclease. Through
CRISPRs, DNA is modified by inducing cuts or breaks in defective genes, using synthetic guide
RNA to identify the DNA target and CRISPR-associated protein nuclease to cleave the DNA.
Then, the gene is removed completely or new DNA is added. This system allows DNA to be cut
precisely at the location of a mutation so the mutant base is replaced with the base that would
normally be at that location.
RNA also can be used therapeutically to enhance or inhibit the synthesis of specific proteins.
To enhance protein synthesis, mRNA is engineered to encode the desired protein. Delivery of
mRNA often is easier than that of DNA and mRNA does not need to be transported to the
nucleus of the cell where the transcriptional machinery resides. Instead, mRNA only needs to
enter the cytoplasm where translation occurs. Because mRNA tends to be degraded quickly,
various modifications to its composition often are used to increase its stability and, depending
on the application, reduce its inflammatory properties. This process produces chemically
modified RNA. RNA can be used for vaccination (eg, the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-
19 vaccines are RNA vaccines) or applications in which short-term expression is therapeutic,
such as initiating tissue regeneration.12
Considerable interest is centered on using ncRNA to inhibit the synthesis of proteins that
contribute to disease. In this context, various small inhibitory RNA drugs recently have been
approved by the FDA for the management of diseases such as hereditary transthyretin-
mediated amyloidosis.13
The regulation of gene expression using short, synthetic molecules of DNA or RNA known as
oligonucleotides also is possible. Typically 18 to 30 nucleotides long, oligonucleotides contain
base sequences that are complementary (ie, antisense) to sequences in target mRNA. The
binding of an antisense oligonucleotide to its target mRNA blocks translation and usually leads
to degradation of the mRNA.14
Genetic Engineering
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Genetics, Gene Expression, and Epigenetics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002109
14/18

It is possible to alter the genetic composition of cells and organisms using highly specific
restriction enzymes that cut DNA at precise sites defined by base sequences in combination
with DNA ligases that reassemble the pieces into recombinant DNA. Gene editing adds an
additional technology for genetic engineering.
These technologies can be used to generate genetically modified organisms for research,
agricultural, industrial, or medical uses.
Modified DNA is introduced into cells using a viral or nonviral vector. The simplest vectors are
small circular DNA plasmids that exist naturally in bacteria and are straightforward to
engineer. The delivery of DNA into a bacterium using a plasmid is called transformation. DNA
delivery into a mammalian cell using a plasmid is called transfection. DNA delivery into a
mammalian cell using a virus is called transduction.
Genetic engineering not only enables the development of vectors for gene therapy but also
allows for the industrial production of large amounts of recombinant proteins for therapeutic
or diagnostic use.
Often, the wild-type gene is modified to improve the yield of a protein or to produce a variant
protein with enhanced properties. The removal of introns to form cDNA is one such
modification. Another is codon optimization. Many amino acids have more than one codon,
and it is possible to alter DNA to include codons that are more effectively translated in the cell
system being used. Yields also can be enhanced by using strong, constitutive promoters in
place of the native promoter that drives gene expression.
Genetic engineering also is used to produce novel proteins not found in nature. The
antirheumatic drug etanercept, in which DNA encoding a tumor necrosis factor-α receptor has
been fused to DNA encoding a portion of an antibody molecule, is an example.
The engineered genes can be expressed in bacterial or mammalian cell lines to produce
recombinant protein. The choice of cell usually depends on the need for posttranslational
processing. For example, bacteria are unable to glycosylate proteins. Therefore, they are
unsuitable for producing recombinant bone morphogenetic protein-2, which is used for bone
healing and whose activity is diminished greatly if it is unglycosylated. Therefore, Chinese
hamster ovary cells are used instead. Conversely, the anti-inflammatory drug anakinra,
although glycosylated in nature, appears to be fully active if produced in an aglycosylated form
by bacteria.

In addition to the important molecular methods that already have been described, several
other methods are important in clinical orthopaedics.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)—A method of selectively amplifying a specific region of
interest in DNA. This method has many clinical applications, from diagnosis to disease
monitoring and prognosis, and aids in the identification of infectious agents.
Reverse transcriptase PCR—A method of measuring the abundance of specific RNA. RNA first
is converted to cDNA by a viral enzyme called reverse transcriptase and is then amplified by
PCR. Products of reverse transcriptase PCR can be detected on a quantitative, real-time basis
via a technique known as real-time reverse transcriptase PCR.
cDNA microarray—Also known as DNA chips, DNA microarrays are used to measure the
expression levels of large numbers of genes simultaneously or to genotype multiple regions
of a genome. To measure RNA, RNA molecules first are converted to cDNA by reverse
transcriptase. A small surface or chip containing thousands of different complementary DNA
fragments is used to capture specific cDNA within the test material. Their abundance is
measured via a fluorescent technique.
DNA sequencing—Currently, a routine, relatively inexpensive technology offered by most
major medical centers, its power and utility have been enhanced by a parallel sequencing
technology known as next-generation sequencing, which offers high throughput and speed.
RNA sequencing—In recent years, the sequencing of RNA has become possible by reverse
transcribing RNA to cDNA, which is sequenced via established DNA sequencing methods.
This process allows the entire transcriptome of a sample to be revealed.
Single-cell DNA and RNA sequencing—Currently, the sequencing of nucleic acids at the
single-cell level is possible.
